references.text: The direct text Jesus quotes: God reveals himself to Moses at the burning bush (βάτος) and says, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" ([ref:Exod 3:2-6|Exodus 3:2-6]). This is the main reference in Jesus' argument for the resurrection—that God refers to himself as the God of the deceased patriarchs in the present tense, showing that they live for him.

God confirms to Moses that he is "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" and that this is his name forever ([ref:Exod 3:15-16|Exodus 3:15-16]). This repetition emphasizes the eternal relationship between God and the patriarchs.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same argument from the burning bush to prove the resurrection to the Sadducees ([ref:Matt 22:31-32|Matthew 22:31-32]).

The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus refers to "the passage about the thornbush" in Moses' writings and quotes the same words from God to prove the resurrection ([ref:Mark 12:26-27|Mark 12:26-27]).

God makes an eternal covenant with Abraham and his descendants, promising to be their God ([ref:Gen 17:7-8|Genesis 17:7-8]). An eternal covenant presupposes that the patriarchs live for God, which supports Jesus' argument for the resurrection.

God reveals himself to Isaac and says, "I am the God of Abraham your father" ([ref:Gen 26:24|Genesis 26:24]). God refers to himself in relation to Abraham after his death, showing that Abraham still lives for God.

God reveals himself to Jacob and says, "I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac" ([ref:Gen 28:13|Genesis 28:13]). Here too, God uses the present tense regarding his relationship with the patriarchs.

The Letter to the Hebrews confirms that God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them ([ref:Heb 11:16|Hebrews 11:16]). This links God's self-designation as "their God" to eternal life and the hope of resurrection.

The following verse that gives the conclusion to Jesus' argument: "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" ([ref:Luke 20:38|Luke 20:38]). This summarizes the point of the quote from the burning bush.
Stephen refers to the same event with the burning bush and quotes God's words: "I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" ([ref:Acts 7:30-32|Acts 7:30-32]).
